chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Ja'far and others, and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah — all together — from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Musadif who said:

A man from our brethren fell gravely ill in Mecca until he was near death. We met Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) on the road, and he said: 'O Musadif, what happened to so-and-so?' I said, 'I left him near death, may I be your sacrifice.' He said: 'Had I been in your place, I would have given him water from the Mizab (the spout of the Ka'bah) to drink.'

So we sought it from everyone but could not find any. While we were in this situation, suddenly a cloud appeared with thunder, lightning, and rain. I went to someone in the mosque, gave him a dirham, and took his drinking cup. Then I took water from the Mizab, brought it to him and gave him to drink from it. I did not leave his side until he had drunk sawiq and recovered, and he was cured after that.

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: A formula of deep reverence: 'may I be your ransom/sacrifice', used by companions when addressing the Imams
key_terms.سَوِيق: Sawiq — a traditional nourishing drink made from roasted barley or wheat flour; commonly used as a restorative food
key_terms.مَاءُ الْمِيزَابِ: Water of the Mizab — the golden spout installed on the Ka'bah that directs rainwater; considered blessed and curative

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of water from the Mizab (spout) of the Ka'bah in Islamic tradition?
ai.summary: Musadif, a companion of Imam al-Sadiq (AS), narrates a miraculous account of healing through the water of the Mizab (the golden spout of the Ka'bah). When a sick brother was near death in Mecca, the Imam prescribed water from the Mizab as a cure. After they could not find any, providence sent rain that filled the Mizab, and the man was healed after drinking it. This hadith highlights the baraka (blessing) associated with sacred sites of the Ka'bah and the Imam's knowledge of remedies.
